sections.body_md:
A vector norm measures the length of one vector. A matrix asks a different question: how much can multiplication by \(A\) stretch a vector? The induced norm, also called the operator norm, is the largest stretch. Take every vector of length 1, apply \(A\), and keep the longest result. Equivalently, look at \(\lVert Ax \rVert / \lVert x \rVert\) for \(x \ne 0\) and take the supremum. The vector norm in the numerator and the vector norm in the denominator are the same one, so each vector norm produces its own matrix norm.

That definition immediately gives the inequality \(\lVert Ax \rVert \le \lVert A \rVert \, \lVert x \rVert\). One particular vector cannot stretch more than the worst vector. The identity matrix has induced norm 1, and a product of matrices satisfies \(\lVert AB \rVert \le \lVert A \rVert \, \lVert B \rVert\).

Three cases have short formulas. The induced 1-norm is the largest absolute column sum. The induced infinity-norm is the largest absolute row sum. The induced 2-norm is the largest singular value of \(A\). For a real symmetric matrix, that singular value is the largest absolute eigenvalue.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[
\lVert A \rVert = \max_{\lVert x \rVert = 1} \lVert Ax \rVert, \qquad \lVert Ax \rVert \le \lVert A \rVert \, \lVert x \rVert.
\]
With absolute values taken entrywise,
\[
\lVert A \rVert_1 = \max_j \sum_i \lvert a_{ij} \rvert, \qquad \lVert A \rVert_\infty = \max_i \sum_j \lvert a_{ij} \rvert, \qquad \lVert A \rVert_2 = \sigma_{\max}(A).
\]
The 2-norm is also \(\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(A^T A)}\). On a real symmetric matrix it equals \(\max_i \lvert \lambda_i(A) \rvert\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(A\) have rows \((8, 0, 0)\) and \((1, 1, 1)\). Absolute column sums are \(8+1 = 9\), \(0+1 = 1\), and \(0+1 = 1\). The induced 1-norm is 9. Absolute row sums are 8 and \(1+1+1 = 3\). The induced infinity-norm is 8.

The two numbers disagree, which is ordinary: column sums and row sums inspect different directions. The induced 2-norm is a third quantity, the largest singular value of this same matrix. It is not defined as the larger of 9 and 8, and it is not equal to the largest entry 8 either. Each formula has to be used for the norm it names.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Swapping rows and columns swaps the 1-norm and the infinity-norm. Taking the largest absolute entry is not an induced norm; the matrix of all ones has largest entry 1 and induced 2-norm 2. A negative eigenvalue still contributes its absolute value to the 2-norm. The Frobenius norm, built from squares of entries, is a genuine matrix norm, but it is not the operator norm induced by the vector 2-norm, and it is at least as large as that operator norm.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: If a gradient is Lipschitz, the Lipschitz constant can be read as an induced norm of a Hessian. For the quadratic \(\tfrac12 x^T A x\) with symmetric \(A\), that constant is exactly \(\lVert A \rVert_2\). A descent lemma then turns the constant into a quadratic upper bound on the function. The Frobenius norm is a different size, useful as a comparison because it sits above the induced 2-norm and is easy to compute from the entries.
